newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. lawmakers want to protect legal immigrants.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. lawmakers want to protect legal immigrants.

text.p: A bipartisan group of legislators proposed a new law Monday that would delay provisions in the Welfare Reform Act that cut off benefits to legal immigrants.

The bill, to be introduced in the Senate by Republican Alfonse D'Amato Wednesday and in the House by Republican Peter King the same day, was designed to give elderly and disabled people more time to become U.S. citizens and avoid losing benefits.

"There are tens of thousands of people who came in here properly and through no fault of their own, because we have this time line of August 22, they won't really be able to have an opportunity to become citizens," D'Amato told a news conference at New York's City Hall.

Under the Welfare Reform Act signed by President Clinton last year, disability and nutrition aid for legal immigrants must be terminated by Aug. 22, 1997. Those who were not on the rolls before August 1986, when the law took effect, are already ineligible for most federal benefit programmes.

More than 40 percent of total savings in the welfare law will come from denying benefits to legal aliens. As the deadline for ending aid to legal immigrants approaches, pressure is building for Congress to act.

Another bill, sponsored by California Democrat Dianne Feinstein, Rhode Island Republican John Chafee and others, was introduced in the Senate last week that would guarantee that legal immigrants who were receiving Food Stamp and disability aid when the welfare law was signed last year will continue to get federal checks.

D'Amato was joined at the news conference by King, New York Democratic Representative Carolyn McCarthy, New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and members of an Immigration Coalition convened by the mayor last year to fight the new laws.
Giuliani has filed two lawsuits in Manhattan federal court since October challenging provisions in the Welform Reform Act and Immigration Reform Act.

The cut-off of Social Security Income coverage and Food Stamps would cost New York City and New York State about $1.4 billion over a six-year period from 1997 through 2002, according to the mayor's office.
